lessons.title: How Seed and Series A Valuations Get Set in Practice

children.text: Ask a finance textbook how to value a company and you get discounted cash flows. Ask a seed investor in Bengaluru and you get something closer to "we usually take 18%, you need about ₹7 crore, so let us call it ₹32 crore pre". Neither side is being lazy. A company with 14 months of history and no predictable cash flow cannot be valued by projecting cash flows into 2034. This lesson shows how the number really gets set, and where you have leverage to move it.

body.text: Early-stage valuation is not a calculation, it is a negotiation dressed as one. The number is driven by how much you need, how much the investor must own, what similar companies priced at, and above all whether anyone else is competing to give you the money.

children.text: The Way It Actually Happens: Work Backwards

Most seed and Series A valuations are reverse-engineered from two numbers that are decided first: how much money the company needs to reach its next milestone, and how much of the company the investor needs to own to make the deal worth their while.

body.caption: The valuation falls out of the other two numbers, not the other way round

children.text: A Hyderabad SaaS company needs ₹7 crore to fund 18 months of hiring. The fund it is talking to targets around 18% ownership at seed. So post-money is ₹7 crore ÷ 0.18 = ₹38.9 crore, which makes pre-money about ₹31.9 crore. Nobody sat down and valued the company. They agreed on a cheque and a stake, and the valuation is simply what those two imply.

stats.label: Amount needed
stats.context: 18 months of runway plus a buffer

stats.label: Stake the fund targets
stats.context: Enough for the fund's own ownership maths to work

body.text: This is why asking for more money at the same valuation is not a free win. If you ask for ₹12 crore instead of ₹7 crore and the investor still needs 18%, the valuation has to rise to about ₹67 crore post, and now you have to justify it. Raise for milestones you can actually hit, not for the largest number you can extract.

body.title: Reverse-engineer the valuation
body.prompt: A founder needs ₹5 crore and the lead investor wants 20% of the company. What pre-money valuation does that imply, in ₹ crore?
body.explanation: Post-money is ₹5 crore ÷ 0.20 = ₹25 crore, so pre-money is ₹25 crore − ₹5 crore = ₹20 crore. Notice that nobody had to defend the number ₹20 crore on its own. It fell out of the amount raised and the stake sold.

children.text: The Sanity Check: Multiples of Revenue
Once a number is on the table, both sides test it against what similar companies priced at. At Series A that usually means a multiple of revenue, because there are no profits to multiply yet.

body.caption: A company at ₹6 crore of ARR priced at ₹90 crore post-money is valued at 15 times revenue
Rough multiple ranges seen in Indian rounds (highly variable, not benchmarks)
headers: What moves it within the range

cells: Growth rate, net revenue retention, gross margin
Take rate, buyer repeat rate, supply lock-in
Contribution margin, repeat rate, share of prepaid orders
Credit quality, collection efficiency, cost of capital
Gross margin, and whether it scales without headcount
Set by team, IP and comparables

body.text: Treat those ranges as weather, not physics. Indian SaaS companies that raised at very high multiples of revenue in 2021 saw comparable businesses priced at a fraction of that by 2023. Same company, same metrics, very different number, because the multiple depends on how much capital is chasing deals that quarter. Never build a plan around a multiple from a boom year.

body.title: Check the multiple
body.prompt: A SaaS startup with ₹4 crore of annual recurring revenue is offered ₹14 crore at a ₹58 crore pre-money valuation. What revenue multiple does the post-money valuation imply?
body.explanation: Post-money is ₹58 crore + ₹14 crore = ₹72 crore. ₹72 crore ÷ ₹4 crore = 18 times ARR. That sits inside the usual Series A band for SaaS, so the real question becomes whether growth and retention justify the upper half of the range or the lower half.

body.label: The strongest lever you control
body.context: Nothing moves valuation like competition. Running a tight process so two or three investors reach a decision in the same fortnight does more for your price than any slide. The second strongest lever is runway, because an investor can always smell a founder who has to close.

body.title: How pre-revenue companies get valued: the scorecard method

children.text: With no revenue to multiply, some angels and angel networks use a scorecard. Start from a base: the typical pre-money valuation of comparable seed deals in the same city and sector, say ₹12 crore. Then adjust factor by factor, where 1.0 means average, above 1.0 means better than average and below 1.0 means worse.

content.caption: Scorecard applied to an illustrative pre-revenue startup

children.text: Pre-money = ₹12 crore × 1.17 = ₹14.04 crore, usually rounded to ₹14 crore. The method looks precise and is not: change the base or a single rating and the answer moves by crores. Its real value is as a structured argument about what makes this company better or worse than the average deal, which is a far more useful discussion than haggling over the final number.
Why Pushing the Number Too High Backfires

markDefs.definition: A funding round priced below the valuation of the previous round. It dilutes existing shareholders heavily and can trigger anti-dilution protection for earlier investors.

children.text: Every valuation sets a bar the next round has to clear. Push the seed to ₹60 crore post when the business supports ₹35 crore, and the Series A must be priced above ₹60 crore. If the company then grows well but not spectacularly, you face a
, which is far more damaging than a modest seed price would ever have been.

body.title: Who has the strongest negotiating position?
body.question: Four founders are discussing valuation with investors. Who has the most leverage on price?
options: The founder with 10 months of runway and two funds running diligence in parallel
The founder with the largest total addressable market slide
The founder with 6 weeks of runway and one interested investor
The founder who raised at the highest valuation in a previous round
body.explanation: Leverage comes from competition and from the ability to walk away, and ten months of runway with two live processes gives both. A large market slide persuades nobody on its own, six weeks of cash with one investor is the weakest possible position, and a high previous valuation is often a burden if the business has not grown into it.

body.title: Two offers, one decision
body.scenario:
Divya's Bengaluru SaaS company has ₹5 crore of ARR, growing 3.4 times year on year, with net revenue retention of 118%. She needs about ₹18 crore to fund 20 months.
Offer A: ₹18 crore at ₹72 crore pre-money, from a fund with deep SaaS experience, a 10% ESOP pool created pre-money, and a standard 1x non-participating preference.
Offer B: ₹18 crore at ₹102 crore pre-money, from a generalist fund new to SaaS, an 18% ESOP pool created pre-money, and a 1x participating preference.
body.prompt: Work out the ownership under each offer and decide which you would take.
body.modelAnswer:
Start with the arithmetic.
Offer A: post-money is ₹72 + ₹18 = ₹90 crore, so the investor takes ₹18 ÷ ₹90 = 20%. The pool takes another 10% pre-money. Founders and existing holders keep roughly 70%. The multiple is ₹90 crore ÷ ₹5 crore = 18 times ARR.
Offer B: post-money is ₹102 + ₹18 = ₹120 crore, so the investor takes ₹18 ÷ ₹120 = 15%. The pool takes 18% pre-money. Founders and existing holders keep roughly 67%. The multiple is ₹120 crore ÷ ₹5 crore = 24 times ARR.
The headline says B is worth ₹30 crore more. The ownership says B leaves the founders with less, because the bigger pool more than swallows the smaller investor stake.
Then the terms. A participating preference means the investor takes their ₹18 crore off the top at exit and then also shares what is left by percentage, which costs the founders real money in any outcome short of a very large exit.
Then the next round. At 24 times ARR, Divya has to grow into a ₹120 crore price. At 18 times she has room.
Answer: take Offer A, and use Offer B as leverage to negotiate the pool down or the price up. If she wants B's number, the conditions are a smaller pool and a non-participating preference. Valuation is one line in a term sheet, not the deal.

body.title: Before you name a number
steps: Work out how much you need for 18 to 24 months of milestones, with a buffer.
Divide that by the stake you are willing to sell, usually 15% to 25%, and see what valuation it implies.
Sanity check the implied multiple against your revenue and against recent comparable rounds.
Ask what ESOP pool is assumed, and whether it sits pre-money or post-money.
Check the preference and other economic terms before comparing headline valuations.
Count your runway. If it is under six months, fix that before you negotiate price.
Line up several conversations so decisions land in the same fortnight.
Decide in advance the lowest valuation and the worst terms you will accept.

body.title: The real driver
body.textWithBlank: The single strongest lever a founder has on valuation is ___ between investors, because price responds to demand far more than to any slide in the deck.
body.explanation: Two interested investors reaching a decision at the same time move the price more than any argument about market size. Everything else, including growth and team quality, works by creating that competition in the first place.

cards.definition: Post-money derived from the amount raised divided by the stake the investor wants, rather than from a valuation model.
Post-money valuation divided by annual revenue, the common sanity check at Series A.
Valuing a pre-revenue startup by adjusting a base comparable valuation using weighted factor ratings.
A round priced below the previous one, which dilutes heavily and can trigger anti-dilution protection.
Recent rounds by similar companies at a similar stage, used to test whether a price is realistic.
More than one investor wanting the same round, the strongest practical driver of valuation.

points: Most early valuations are reverse-engineered: the amount needed divided by the stake the investor wants gives post-money.
Asking for more money at the same valuation does not work, because the investor's target ownership pushes the price up with it.
Revenue multiples are a sanity check, not a formula, and the usable range shifts with the funding climate.
Multiples from a boom year are not a plan. Indian SaaS was priced very differently in 2021 and 2023 on identical metrics.
Competition between investors moves price more than anything in your deck, and runway is what lets you use that leverage.
Pre-revenue methods like the scorecard are structured conversations, not precise valuations.
A valuation pushed too high sets a bar your next round must clear, and a down round costs far more than a modest price would have.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment, legal or financial advice. Multiple ranges, target ownership levels and scorecard weights are rough market observations that vary widely by sector, stage, investor and funding conditions, and are not benchmarks. Divya's company and all figures are illustrative. Speak to a qualified professional before agreeing any funding terms.
